title: Weekly Briefing: Employee Engagement Hits a 15-Year Low, Microsoft Offers 60,000 Buyouts, and Can Employees Opt Out of AI at Work?
author: Jacob Morgan
summary: Jacob Morgan's Future Ready Leadership Weekly Briefing is a curated digest with editorial commentary on three workplace stories, plus a short podcast note. The first covers Gallup data showing U.S. employee engagement at 29%, the lowest since 2011, which Morgan reads as a failure of clarity, manager support and purpose rather than of perks. The second covers Microsoft's voluntary exit offer to roughly 60,000 employees, where he finds the mechanism more interesting than the number because it gives people agency over restructuring. The third covers a University of Kentucky administrator who obtained a religious accommodation to avoid AI, which Morgan uses to argue that organizations must define when AI is optional, encouraged or necessary. The episode note highlights Merck's Khadija Ben Hammada on performing today while transforming for tomorrow, and on the difference between transparency and clarity. Because the email carries Morgan's own editorial framing of each item, it is archived as a roundup summary; the underlying articles were linked only by name and were not expanded.
points: Morgan ties falling engagement to basic management fundamentals (clear expectations, manager support, purpose, line of sight to strategy) rather than to perks or programs.
Voluntary exit programs reframe restructuring from something done to employees into a choice, which changes the company-employee relationship even though business pressure remains.
Organizations should state explicitly when AI use is optional, encouraged or required, rather than leaving adoption as an unwritten rule.
Technology can be introduced quickly, but explaining what change means for each role and career takes far more deliberate leadership.
Leaders must perform today while building the skills and culture for tomorrow, and employees need clarity about change even when leaders lack every answer.
quotes: None of these stories can be explained by technology alone. They are about trust, clarity, choice, and whether employees still understand where they fit inside an organization that keeps changing.

Engagement is tied to much more basic things: knowing what is expected of you, feeling supported by your manager, understanding why your work matters, and believing there is some connection between what you do and where the organization is going.
Companies can introduce technology quickly. Helping people understand what those changes mean for their role, career, and future takes much more deliberate leadership.
Most workforce restructuring happens to employees. A voluntary exit gives people some agency in deciding whether they still want to be part of what the organization is becoming.
As organizations rethink roles, skills, layers, and operating models, traditional layoffs cannot be the only tool available. Sometimes the answer will be reskilling. Sometimes redeployment.

Organizations will need to become much clearer about when AI is optional, when it is encouraged, and when it is genuinely necessary to perform the job. Adoption cannot simply become an unwritten rule that employees are expected to figure out themselves.
Leaders may not always have every answer, but employees still need to understand what change means for them and how the organization is approaching it.
Leaders still have to deliver results, but at the same time they have to build the skills, capabilities, culture, and organization the business will need next.
